title: Minimize the accessibility of classes and members
concept: Information hiding (encapsulation) is one of the fundamental tenets of good software design. It decouples the components that comprise a system, allowing them to be developed, tested, optimized, understood, and modified in isolation. The rule of thumb is simple: make each class or member as inaccessible as possible. Public classes should have no public fields (except static final constants of immutable objects), and public static final array fields are almost always a major security flaw because non-zero length arrays are always mutable.

when_to_use_flashcard.front: What access level should you choose when declaring a member or class?
when_to_use_flashcard.back: The lowest possible access level: start with private. If another class in the same package needs access, make it package-private. Only make it protected or public if it is part of the exported API.

when_not_to_use_flashcard.front: Why is `public static final Thing[] VALUES = { ... };` almost always a critical design bug?
when_not_to_use_flashcard.back: Because arrays in Java are always mutable! While the reference `VALUES` cannot be reassigned, the contents `VALUES[i]` can be modified by any client in the JVM. Use `Collections.unmodifiableList` or return defensive clones.

quiz.question: What is the four-level access control hierarchy in Java, ordered from least to most accessible?
options: private, package-private (default), protected, public
private, protected, package-private, public
package-private, private, protected, public
private, internal, protected, public

quiz.question: What happens if a method overrides a superclass method regarding access level modifiers?
options: The overriding method cannot have a more restrictive access level than the superclass method (Liskov Substitution Principle)
The overriding method must have the exact same modifier
The overriding method can be private regardless of superclass access
Overriding methods do not inherit access rules

quiz.question: Under what circumstance may a public class have a public field?
options: Only when the field is static final and refers to an immutable object or primitive value
Whenever the field is marked volatile
When the class implements Serializable
Whenever the field is a non-empty array

quiz.question: How did Java 9's Module System (JPMS) expand access control boundaries?
options: A public class or member in a module is only accessible outside the module if its package is explicitly exported in module-info.java
It removed the package-private modifier
It made all private fields accessible globally
It replaced protected with internal

quiz.question: What is an acceptable reason to broaden an access level from private to package-private?
options: To allow a package-adjacent unit test to inspect or exercise internal state
To allow any arbitrary external library to modify the field
To improve garbage collection throughput
To enable JIT compilation

interview_questions.question: Why is information hiding (encapsulation) so crucial to building large software systems?
interview_questions.model_answer: Encapsulation decouples components, allowing each to be modified, tested, profiled, and reasoned about independently. It enables parallel team development, isolates bugs, allows safe internal optimizations without breaking client code, and reduces security attack surfaces.

interview_questions.question: A library contains `public static final String[] ALLOWED_IPS = {"10.0.0.1", "10.0.0.2"};`. What security hazard exists?
interview_questions.model_answer: The `final` keyword only prevents reassigning the `ALLOWED_IPS` array reference; it does not protect the array contents. Any external code in the JVM can execute `ALLOWED_IPS[0] = "192.168.1.1"` and overwrite authorized IP addresses, completely bypassing firewall checks.

interview_questions.question: Why shouldn't you make a member `protected` lightly?
interview_questions.model_answer: A protected member is part of the class's exported public API because anyone can subclass your class and access it. Furthermore, protected members in Java are accessible to all other classes in the same package. Once declared protected, you must maintain and support it indefinitely.

interview_questions.question: What are the two safe alternatives to public array constants?
interview_questions.model_answer:
1. Make the array private and expose a `public static final List<T>` wrapped with `Collections.unmodifiableList(Arrays.asList(ARRAY))` (or `List.of(...)` in Java 9+).
2. Make the array private and expose a public accessor method that returns a defensive copy: `return ARRAY.clone();`.
